summary: TerraMatch Chile is a reproducible, explainable method and prototype for screening Chile for partial analogs of specific lunar and Martian terrains. We built reference relief profiles for western Elysium Planitia (Mars, MGS MOLA MEGDR) and Mare Tranquillitatis (Moon, SLDEM2015 from LRO LOLA and SELENE/Kaguya) and compared them with a 31,660-cell grid of Chile using ASTER GDEM v3. Only physically comparable variables enter the score (90th-percentile slope, local relief and roughness), computed at a common 463 m resolution in 5 km windows, after pre-filters for aridity (GPM IMERG V07) and volcanic lithology. In a first real run over four pilot ASTER tiles, the model clearly separated steep from flat terrain: the Llullaillaco control ranked in the 8th percentile. It also showed that Yungay and Salar de Pajonales, well-known Mars analogs for aridity and soil chemistry, are not relief analogs of Elysium Planitia at this scale. Analogy depends on the variable and the scale, and TerraMatch makes that explicit for every candidate.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

TerraMatch Chile identifies, characterizes and ranks Chilean environments that may serve as partial analogs of lunar and Martian terrains. It never claims that a place is identical to the Moon or Mars, and it does not assess landing safety, base siting or habitability. It answers a narrower question: which Chilean environments share measurable relief characteristics with a given planetary reference region, in which dimensions they differ, and what research or mission-preparation activities they could support.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Planetary reference profiles. We use a 30 x 30 km pilot area in western Elysium Planitia (4.50 N, 135.90 E, near the InSight landing ellipse) and one in Mare Tranquillitatis (0.674 N, 23.473 E, Apollo 11 site). These are reference regions for analysis, not proposed base locations. Each area is split into 25 windows of 5 km. The reference value is the median of the windows, and the range runs from the 10th to the 90th percentile. Only 30.6% of MOLA pixels in the Mars area are direct measurements, so we use only the 5 windows with at least 50% measured pixels; using all 25 changes the median slope by less than 0.06 degrees. Mars profile: slope P90 0.45 degrees, local relief 15 m, roughness 0.15 degrees. Moon profile (25 windows): slope P90 1.17 degrees, local relief 59 m, roughness 0.42 degrees.

2. Harmonization. All three elevation models are resampled to 463 m (the MOLA MEGDR resolution) before slope is computed in a metric projection (UTM 18S/19S in Chile, maximum scale error 0.053%), because slope depends on resolution. Absolute elevation is reported but never compared, since each body has a different vertical datum.

3. Pre-filters. For Mars, only cells with mean annual precipitation of 250 mm or less (GPM IMERG V07, 2001-2024) are ranked. For the Moon, only Pliocene-Quaternary volcanic units of the SERNAGEOMIN 1:1,000,000 geological map are considered. Excluded cells are shown as "outside filter", not as "low similarity".

4. Similarity score. For each variable, the distance is zero inside the reference range. Outside it, the distance to the nearest edge is divided by the variable's interquartile range across Chile. Similarity S = 100 x exp(-D), with equal weights. Missing data is never set to zero, and a 5 km window with less than 50% valid pixels is left empty.

5. Robustness. 500 Monte Carlo runs perturb the reference values and the weights (Dirichlet, concentration 20). We report how often each candidate ranks in the top 1% (p_top) and its p05-p95 rank range, which set its confidence level (High, Medium or Low).

6. Validation. Yungay and Salar de Pajonales are known Mars analogs (benchmarks). Llullaillaco and the steepest 5% of cells are negative controls. The Llaima lava-flow sector is an exploratory lunar candidate, with the Llaima cone as an internal contrast.

RESULTS (FIRST RUN WITH REAL DATA)

The run used four pilot ASTER tiles over Atacama and Llaima: 1,262 cells with full relief data, 895 scored against Mars and 256 against the Moon. It is not a national ranking.

- Llullaillaco, Mars control (target: percentile 25 or lower): 8.3, passed.

- Steepest 5% of cells, Mars control (target: percentile 25 or lower): 2.5, passed.

- Yungay, Mars benchmark (target: percentile 75 or higher): 47.4, not passed.

- Salar de Pajonales, Mars benchmark (target: percentile 75 or higher): 63.1, not passed.

- Llaima lava flows vs. cone, Moon (target: flows more similar): S 39.0 vs. 17.2, passed.

The model separates steep terrain from flat terrain well. Elysium Planitia is extremely smooth at this scale (slope P90 0.45 degrees, relief 15 m), while Yungay (8.2 degrees, 173 m) and Pajonales (7.4 degrees, 155 m) are much rougher. They are Mars analogs because of aridity and soil chemistry, not because of their relief at 5 km scale, and we report this failed benchmark as found. The Llaima flows resemble Mare Tranquillitatis more than the cone does, but they are still much steeper (11.8 degrees against 0.9-2.5), so this is a relative result. All five sites have Low confidence in the Monte Carlo (p_top = 0). Results hold when CR2MET v2.0 replaces IMERG as the rainfall source (percentiles 47.3 and 63.0). The cells most similar to Elysium cluster near 24.5 S, 68.9 W; their landform has not yet been identified on satellite imagery.

BENEFITS AND EXPECTED IMPACT

A transparent, reproducible way to screen a whole country for analog candidates, beyond already-famous sites. Every score is explainable variable by variable, and every variable links to its source. It also shows when a famous analog is not similar in a given dimension. This helps researchers and mission planners choose field sites for rover mobility tests, instrument trials, sampling practice and geology training, and it puts Chile's diversity of deserts, salt flats, volcanoes and glaciers on the map of planetary analog research.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Instead of declaring one famous site "Mars-like", TerraMatch turns analog selection into a measurable test that can fail. It scores every 5 km cell of a country against a planetary profile, uses the same code and the same scale for Earth, Mars and the Moon, and keeps the filters separate from the score. Our most interesting finding came from a failed test: the classic Atacama analogs are not relief analogs of Elysium Planitia at 5 km, which shows that analogy depends on the variable and the scale.

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

Only variables that measure the same quantity on both bodies enter the score, at one common resolution. Data quality is reported, not hidden: MOLA interpolation, IMERG's rainfall bias in the desert and the third-party copy of the geological map. Missing data is never treated as zero. A Monte Carlo analysis shows how stable each ranking is. The scope was kept realistic for a 36-hour hackathon: two planetary profiles, five Chilean sites and four pilot tiles. AI assistance is declared and no NASA branding is used.

LIMITATIONS

Only 4 of about 160 ASTER tiles for Chile were processed, so percentiles may change with full coverage. Similarity is topographic only and does not imply geological, thermal or material similarity. The 463 m resolution cannot capture rover-scale obstacles. The Pajonales and Llaima-flow polygons come from 1:1,000,000 map units, not from image digitization. No Earth site reproduces reduced gravity, vacuum, radiation or the thin Martian atmosphere, and Mare Tranquillitatis does not represent the lunar polar regions relevant to permanent bases. Next steps: full national coverage, the lunar south pole, more Martian regions and thermal variables.

TOOLS

Python 3 with NumPy, pandas, SciPy, rasterio, pyproj, GeoPandas, Shapely and Matplotlib; Jupyter for exploratory analysis; GitHub. Reproducible pipeline: tests/test_pipeline_synthetic.py, src/features/chile_features.py, src/run_pipeline.py, figures/make_figures.py. [PENDIENTE: Marti — app framework and hosting].
